title: Sunrise: the 'beauteous mere' and the 'brazen heaven'
greek: Ἠέλιος δ᾽ ἀνόρουσε, λιπὼν περικαλλέα λίμνην, οὐρανὸν ἐς πολύχαλκον (Ēelios d' anorouse, lipōn perikallea limnēn, ouranon es poluchalkon)
short: The sun springs up from the 'mere', the stream of Ocean, into a sky of bronze; Book 3 opens with a cosmic image instead of the usual dawn formula.
body: Merry and Riddell explain limnē, usually 'lake' or 'pool', as used here of the Ocean stream from which the sun rises, comparing passages where it means a bay or the open sea. Polychalkos, 'of much bronze', describes the sky: older commentators took it as 'solid, firm' (like Pindar's 'bronze heaven, an ever-secure seat', Nemean 6.3-4, and our 'firmament'), others as 'bright-flashing'. Merry and Riddell prefer the picture of a vault of burnished metal and compare Job 37:18, 'the sky, which is strong, and as a molten looking glass'. The sun gives light 'to the immortals and to mortal men on the earth, the giver of grain' (zeidōros aroura), a formula for the life-giving earth that recurs at 4.229.

anchor: Pylos, the well-built citadel of Neleus
title: Pylos, city of Neleus and Nestor
greek: Πύλον, Νηλῆος ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον (Pulon, Nēlēos euktimenon ptoliethron)
short: Nestor's sandy Pylos in the western Peloponnese; where it lay was disputed in antiquity, and the excavation of a Mycenaean palace near modern Pylos in 1939 transformed the debate.
body: Neleus, Nestor's father, founded the kingdom. Merry and Riddell report the ancient controversy over which of three places called Pylos was Nestor's: the Eleian, the Triphylian, or the Messenian. Strabo argued for Triphylian Pylos, partly because Homer associates Nestor's kingdom with the river Alpheus (Iliad 5.545). In 1939 Carl Blegen found the so-called Palace of Nestor at Ano Englianos in Messenia, with archives of Linear B tablets that name the place pu-ro, Pylos, and record offerings to Poseidon. Most scholars now place Homer's Pylos there, though the poems' geography is not always consistent. The epithet 'sandy' (ēmathoeis, 1.93, 2.214) fits the Messenian coast.

title: Black bulls for the 'dark-haired Earth-shaker'
greek: ταύρους παμμέλανας, ἐνοσίχθονι κυανοχαίτῃ (taurous pammelanas, enosichthoni kuanochaitēi)
short: The Pylians sacrifice all-black bulls to Poseidon, 'dark-haired' (kyanochaitēs), god of earthquakes and patron of Nestor's family.
body: Kuanos is a dark blue-black substance (perhaps blue glass paste or lapis), and Merry and Riddell render the epithet as the colour Tennyson called 'blue-black hair'; it is used of Hades and of a horse as well. Black victims normally went to the gods of the underworld (11.33) or to Earth (Iliad 3.103). Merry and Riddell suggest the colour here either symbolizes the dark sea or reflects Poseidon's awesome power, which puts him on a level with the chthonic gods; they note that elsewhere (Pindar, Virgil) Poseidon receives a white bull, and that a Boeotian title of the god was 'Taureos'. Nestor's line descends from Poseidon through Neleus (11.235-257), which explains the scale of the festival. The scene also sets Telemachus, son of Poseidon's enemy, among the god's worshippers.

title: Nine companies of five hundred: the Pylian festival
greek: ἐννέα δ᾽ ἕδραι ἔσαν, πεντακόσιοι δ᾽ ἐν ἑκάστῃ ἥατο, καὶ προὔχοντο ἑκάστοθι ἐννέα ταύρους (ennea d' hedrai esan, pentakosioi d' en hekastēi hēato …)
short: Nine groups of five hundred men, each offering nine bulls: 4,500 worshippers and eighty-one victims.
body: Merry and Riddell explain hedrai as 'messes' or seated companies and note that the nine correspond to the nine Pylian towns (Iliad 2.591-594); ancient scholia say Nestor ruled nine cities. Five hundred to each company gives 4,500 men, which, they observe, matches the crews of Nestor's ninety ships at Troy at fifty men a ship (Iliad 2.602, 2.719). The numbers are formal and symmetrical (nine by nine) rather than realistic, and they make the first scene of Book 3 a picture of a whole people at worship, in contrast to the disorderly feasting of the suitors in Ithaca. Telemachus arrives just as they have tasted the entrails and are burning the thigh-pieces.

title: Splanchna and thigh-pieces: the order of sacrifice
greek: εὖθ᾽ οἱ σπλάγχνα πάσαντο, θεῷ δ᾽ ἐπὶ μηρί᾽ ἔκαιον (euth' hoi splanchna pasanto, theōi d' epi mēri' ekaion)
short: The splanchna (heart, liver, lungs, kidneys) were roasted and tasted first by the participants, while the thigh-bones wrapped in fat were burned for the god.
body: Homeric sacrifice follows a fixed sequence, laid out fully later in this book (3.430-463): preliminary washing and barley, prayer, the killing, the women's cry, the cutting out of the thigh-bones (mēria) wrapped in a double layer of fat with raw flesh laid on them, burning these for the god with libations of wine, tasting the splanchna roasted on five-pronged forks, then roasting and eating the rest of the meat. Merry and Riddell refer the reader forward to that passage. Hesiod explains the gods' portion of bones and fat by Prometheus' trick at Mecone (Theogony 535-557). Walter Burkert interpreted the communal eating of the entrails as the moment that binds the participants together in the act of killing.

title: Aidōs: the young man's shame
greek: οὐ μέν σε χρὴ ἔτ᾽ αἰδοῦς, οὐδ᾽ ἠβαιόν … αἰδὼς δ᾽ αὖ νέον ἄνδρα γεραίτερον ἐξερέεσθαι (ou men se chrē et' aidous … aidōs d' au neon andra geraiteron exereesthai)
short: Telemachus feels aidōs, the shame or respectful reserve of a young man before an elder; Athena tells him he has no more need of it.
body: Aidōs is a central Greek social emotion: a sense of shame, modesty or respect that restrains a person from improper behaviour, especially before superiors, guests or the gods. It can be a virtue, but here it is an obstacle, and Athena encourages Telemachus to speak: 'somewhat thou wilt of thyself devise ... and somewhat heaven too will prompt thee' (3.26-27). Merry and Riddell comment on the construction in 3.24, where the noun is drawn into the accusative by the infinitive, and compare similar phrases in Aeschylus. Douglas Cairns' study traces the concept from Homer onward. Telemachus' progress from shy silence to confident speech is one of the main threads of the Telemachy; Nestor soon remarks that his speech is like his father's (3.123-125).

title: Peisistratus, son of Nestor
greek: Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος (Nestoridēs Peisistratos)
short: Nestor's youngest son, Telemachus' companion on the road to Sparta; his name was later borne by the Athenian tyrant, whose family claimed descent from Nestor's line.
body: Merry and Riddell suggest Peisistratus was the youngest of Nestor's six surviving sons (the seventh, Antilochus, fell at Troy, 4.187-188), and that Thrasymedes, seated next to his father, was the eldest. Peisistratus is Telemachus' age-mate and first friend: he welcomes the strangers, gives the cup first to the older 'Mentor', which pleases Athena (3.52-53), and drives Telemachus to Sparta. In Book 4 his tactful speech about weeping and his grief for Antilochus show him as a model of courtesy. Herodotus reports that the Athenian tyrant Peisistratus belonged to a family that claimed descent from the Neleids of Pylos and was named after Nestor's son (5.65.3-4), so the name carried political weight in Athens, where the Homeric poems were recited at the Panathenaea.

title: The aegis: 'Zeus who bears the aegis'
greek: κούρην Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο (kourēn Dios aigiochoio)
short: Aigiochos, 'aegis-bearing', is a standing title of Zeus; the aegis is his terrifying tasselled goatskin (or shield), which Athena also wears.
body: The aegis (aigis) was understood by the Greeks as a goatskin (aix, 'goat'), and the epithet aigiochos as 'holding the aegis'; some ancient and modern scholars connect it instead with kataigis, 'storm-wind', making Zeus the 'driver of the storm'. In the Iliad the aegis is a fearful object with a hundred golden tassels and the Gorgon's head at its centre (Iliad 5.738-742); Hephaestus made it for Zeus, and when it is shaken armies panic (Iliad 15.307-310, 17.593-596). Athena wears it in battle, and in the Odyssey she raises it from the roof of the hall to rout the suitors (22.297-298). The formula 'daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis' is used of Athena throughout Books 3-4 (3.394, 4.752, 4.762), reminding us that the gentle guide of Telemachus is also a goddess of war.

title: Athena prays to Poseidon, and answers her own prayer
greek: ὣς ἄρ᾽ ἔπειτ᾽ ἠρᾶτο καὶ αὐτὴ πάντα τελεύτα (hōs ar' epeit' ērato kai autē panta teleuta)
short: Disguised as Mentor, Athena pours a libation and prays to Poseidon for the Pylians and for a safe return, 'and was herself fulfilling all'.
body: Peisistratus hands the cup first to the older guest, 'for all men have need of the gods' (3.48), and Athena 'rejoiced at the man's wisdom and judgment'. Her prayer is correct in form, but the narrator's comment, that she herself brought everything to pass, adds a layer of irony: a goddess prays to her uncle while silently granting what she asks. The scene also teaches Telemachus by example how a guest behaves at a sacrifice, before he must pray in turn. Commentators note the delicacy of the situation, since Poseidon is Odysseus' enemy and Athena's rival; she addresses him with full courtesy. Merry and Riddell, on a related passage, note that eidomenē expresses real physical likeness: the Pylians see Mentor.

title: The depas amphikypellon
greek: δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον (depas amphikupellon)
short: A standard Homeric drinking cup whose shape is disputed: 'two-handled' (Aristarchus) or a 'double cup' joined base to base (Buttmann).
body: Merry and Riddell set out the debate. Buttmann argued that amphikypellon means a double cup, like two cups set base to base, so that it could stand on either end. Aristarchus took it as a cup with two handles, and Heinrich Schliemann claimed to have found the Homeric type at Troy in tall, trumpet-shaped goblets with two large handles; Merry and Riddell find some of Schliemann's arguments weak. Murray follows the two-handled view. Archaeologists still use 'depas amphikypellon' as the name for the two-handled goblets of Troy II and related Early Bronze Age sites, though the identification with Homer's cup is not certain. The question is a classic case of the attempt to match Homeric objects with excavated finds.

title: 'The horseman, Nestor of Gerenia'
greek: Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ (Gerēnios hippota Nestōr)
short: Nestor's standing title: 'the Gerenian horseman'. He is the oldest of the Greek kings, said to have ruled through three generations of men.
body: Gerēnios was explained in antiquity from Gerenia (or Gerena), a place in Messenia where Nestor was being brought up when Heracles sacked Pylos and killed his eleven brothers; the explanation may be a later guess. Hippota, 'horseman', recalls Nestor's youthful exploits as a charioteer, which he narrates in the Iliad (11.670-761). Telemachus says 'thrice, men say, has he been king for a generation of men' (3.245). Merry and Riddell note the odd middle form of the verb in that line and compare Iliad 1.250-252, where Nestor has outlived two generations and rules among the third. In the Odyssey he is the model of the hero who came home and lives in prosperity and piety among his sons, a contrast to both Agamemnon and Odysseus; Menelaus later describes his blessed old age (4.207-211).

title: 'Are you traders or pirates?'
greek: ἤ τι κατὰ πρῆξιν ἦ μαψιδίως ἀλάλησθε οἷά τε ληιστῆρες ὑπεὶρ ἅλα (ē ti kata prēxin ē mapsidiōs alalēsthe hoia te lēistēres hupeir hala)
short: Nestor asks the strangers, after feeding them, whether they travel on business or roam the sea like pirates; Thucydides cited the question as proof that piracy was once no disgrace.
body: The same lines are spoken by the Cyclops (9.252-255) and in Apollo's Hymn (Homeric Hymn to Apollo 452-455). Thucydides, describing early Greece, says that the old poets show people asking arriving sailors whether they are pirates, without the question being an insult to those asked or a reproach from those who wished to know (1.5.2). Raiding by sea was an accepted way of acquiring wealth in the heroic world; Odysseus himself sacks Ismarus (9.39-61) and boasts of raids in his lying tales (14.229-234). The question also follows the rules of hospitality: Nestor asks only after the guests have eaten (3.69-70), as Telemachus did with Mentes.

title: Amphitrite, the sea
greek: μετὰ κύμασιν Ἀμφιτρίτης (meta kumasin Amphitritēs)
short: Amphitrite in Homer is hardly more than a name for the sea itself; later she is Poseidon's wife and queen of the sea.
body: Merry and Riddell note that 'so far as Amphitrite is personified in Homer, she is the representative of the sea itself rather than a goddess', and cite Dissen's observation that the waves and sea-monsters are called hers, not Poseidon's (3.91; 5.422; 12.60, 12.97). The etymology is obscure: the name has been linked with the sea's moaning round the shores, or with the root seen in Triton and Tritogeneia (compare 3.378). In Hesiod (Theogony 243, 930-933) she is a Nereid and the wife of Poseidon, mother of Triton. Telemachus pictures his father dying either on land at the hands of enemies or 'on the deep among the waves of Amphitrite', with no grave or news.

title: 'I come to your knees': the language of supplication
greek: τοὔνεκα νῦν τὰ σὰ γούναθ᾽ ἱκάνομαι (touneka nun ta sa gounath' hikanomai)
short: Telemachus says he comes 'to the knees' of Nestor: the formula of the suppliant, used here as a polite and urgent request rather than a literal clasping of knees.
body: In full supplication (hiketeia) the suppliant clasps the knees, chin or hand of the person entreated and places himself under the protection of Zeus Hikesios; John Gould's classic article describes the ritual and its obligations. Telemachus uses the phrase figuratively, as do others in the poem, to show that he asks a favour that the hearer is bound in honour to grant. He repeats the same speech, almost word for word, to Menelaus (4.322-331), a sign of formulaic composition and of his growing confidence in a set role. He also asks for the truth, not soothing words, a request that defines the Telemachy as a quest for knowledge of his father.

title: 'There lies Aias, there Achilles': the dead of Troy
greek: ἔνθα μὲν Αἴας κεῖται ἀρήιος, ἔνθα δ᾽ Ἀχιλλεύς, ἔνθα δὲ Πάτροκλος … ἔνθα δ᾽ ἐμὸς φίλος υἱός (entha men Aias keitai arēios …)
short: Nestor's lament names the great dead: Ajax son of Telamon, Akhilleus, Patroclus, and his own son Antilochus. The Odyssey recalls events after the Iliad's end.
body: Merry and Riddell note that Aias standing alone, without patronymic, always means the Telamonian Ajax, not his Locrian namesake. His suicide after losing the arms of Akhilleus to Odysseus was told in the Cyclic Little Iliad and is recalled in the Underworld (11.543-567). Akhilleus' death and funeral were narrated in the Aethiopis and are described at 24.36-94. Antilochus was killed by Memnon, son of Dawn, defending his father (4.187-188; Pindar, Pythian 6.28-42). The anaphora 'there ... there ... there' gives the passage the rhythm of a dirge. The Odyssey often presupposes stories later collected in the Epic Cycle, and Nestor's memories make the Trojan war present as recent history.

anchor: fell wrath of the flashing-eyed goddess
title: The wrath of Athena and the quarrel of the Atreidae
greek: μήνιος ἐξ ὀλοῆς γλαυκώπιδος ὀβριμοπάτρης (mēnios ex oloēs glaukōpidos obrimopatrēs)
short: After the sack of Troy Athena's anger (mēnis) split the Greek leaders: Menelaus wanted to sail at once, Agamemnon to stay and appease her with hecatombs.
body: Merry and Riddell explain that Athena's wrath was aimed first at the Locrian Ajax for his outrage on Cassandra in her temple and then at the Greeks generally for leaving it unpunished (compare 1.326-327; Virgil, Aeneid 1.39-45). The word mēnis is the solemn divine anger of the first line of the Iliad. Nestor describes an assembly called 'recklessly and in no due order, at set of sun', with the men 'heavy with wine' (3.137-139), a picture of disorder that recalls the suitors. Agamemnon's hope of appeasing the goddess is called folly: 'the mind of the gods that are forever is not quickly turned' (3.147). The quarrel divides the fleet and begins the scattered returns. Jenny Strauss Clay made Athena's ambivalent anger a key to the poem.

title: 'Shepherd of the host' (poimēn laōn)
greek: Ἀγαμέμνονι, ποιμένι λαῶν (Agamemnoni, poimeni laōn)
short: A traditional title of kings: the ruler is the shepherd of his people, responsible for protecting and feeding them.
body: Poimēn laōn is used dozens of times in Homer, most often of Agamemnon. The image of the king as shepherd is very old and widespread in the Near East: Hammurabi calls himself the shepherd of his people in the prologue to his laws, and the Hebrew Bible uses the same figure (2 Samuel 5:2; Ezekiel 34). In the Odyssey the formula sharpens an irony: Odysseus' people, without their shepherd, are being devoured by the suitors, and Agamemnon, the 'shepherd of the host', is butchered 'as one slays an ox at the stall' (4.535). Murray varies the rendering between 'shepherd of the host' and 'shepherd of the people' (3.469, 4.24).

title: The voyage home: Tenedos, Lesbos, Chios and Geraestus
greek: ἐς Τένεδον … ἢ καθύπερθε Χίοιο … παιπαλοέσσης (es Tenedon … ē kathuperthe Chioio … paipaloessēs)
short: Nestor traces the route home across the Aegean: from Troy to Tenedos, then to Lesbos, then straight across the open sea to Geraestus, the southern cape of Euboea.
body: Merry and Riddell note that Tenedos, the island off the Trojan coast, was the first day's journey. At Lesbos the leaders debated whether to sail north of rugged (paipaloessa) Chios, past the island of Psyria, or along the mainland coast inside it past windy Mimas; they asked a god for a sign and were told to cut straight across the open sea to Euboea. Merry and Riddell explain paipaloessa as 'rugged' with upheaved rock. At Geraestus they sacrificed to Poseidon in thanks. The passage reflects real sailing knowledge of the Aegean and the risks of crossing open water. Odysseus turned back from Tenedos to rejoin Agamemnon (3.162-164), which is where his own wanderings begin.

anchor: Myrmidons that rage with the spear
title: Other homecomings: Neoptolemus, Philoctetes, Idomeneus
greek: Μυρμιδόνας … ἐγχεσιμώρους … Φιλοκτήτην, Ποιάντιον ἀγλαὸν υἱόν (Murmidonas … enchesimōrous … Philoktētēn, Poiantion aglaon huion)
short: Nestor reports the safe returns he has heard of: the Myrmidons under Akhilleus' son Neoptolemus, Philoctetes son of Poias, and Idomeneus to Crete.
body: The Myrmidons were Akhilleus' people from Phthia; after his death they were led by his son Neoptolemus, whose marriage to Menelaus' daughter is being celebrated when Telemachus reaches Sparta (4.5-9). Enchesimōroi, 'spear-raging' in Murray, is an obscure compound: Merry and Riddell list the ancient and modern explanations ('mad with the spear', 'famous for the spear', 'having their lot in the spear') without a decision. Philoctetes, abandoned on Lemnos with his snake-bitten foot (Iliad 2.718-725), was brought to Troy because his bow was needed, a story dramatized by Sophocles. Merry and Riddell note the patronymic adjective Poiantios as an Aeolic feature. Idomeneus' safe return contrasts with a later tradition of exile. The list sets up the contrast with Agamemnon's homecoming that follows.

title: Unburied Aegisthus: the dishonour of the corpse
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄρα τόν γε κύνες τε καὶ οἰωνοὶ κατέδαψαν κείμενον ἐν πεδίῳ ἑκὰς ἄστεος (all' ara ton ge kunes te kai oiōnoi katedapsan …)
short: Had Menelaus found Aegisthus alive, the murderer would have had no burial mound: dogs and birds would have torn him on the plain, and no woman would have mourned him.
body: Denial of burial is the worst disgrace in the Homeric world. The phrase 'dogs and birds' recalls the proem of the Iliad (1.4-5), where the wrath of Akhilleus makes heroes 'a prey for dogs and all birds', and the Iliad's long struggle over the bodies of Patroclus and Hector. Nestor's hypothetical punishment shows how monstrous Aegisthus' deed was felt to be. It also contrasts with the funeral rites that Telemachus is told to perform for his father if he is dead (1.291-292), and with Menelaus' cenotaph mound for Agamemnon in Egypt (4.584). In the event Orestes did hold a funeral feast for Aegisthus and Clytemnestra (3.309-310).

title: The minstrel who guarded Clytemnestra
greek: πὰρ δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἔην καὶ ἀοιδὸς ἀνήρ, ᾧ πόλλ᾽ ἐπέτελλεν Ἀτρεΐδης Τροίηνδε κιὼν εἴρυσθαι ἄκοιτιν (par d' ar' eēn kai aoidos anēr …)
short: Agamemnon left a bard to watch over Clytemnestra; Aegisthus marooned him on a desert island before he could seduce her.
body: This strange detail makes the singer a moral guardian. Merry and Riddell quote Athenaeus' explanation (via Eustathius) that the bard was a 'guardian and counsellor' who first praised the virtues of women to inspire a love of goodness, and then gave pleasant pastime to keep the queen's mind from evil thoughts. They also report a story, attributed to Timolaus, that he was Phemius' brother, and the objection that Odysseus set no such guard over Penelope. The episode belongs to the Odyssey's recurrent interest in singers (Phemius, Demodocus) and suggests the power of song to shape conduct. Nestor adds that Clytemnestra at first refused 'the unseemly deed', for she had good sense, until 'the doom of the gods' bound her.

title: Apollo's 'gentle shafts' at Sunium
greek: Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος κατέπεφνε (Phoibos Apollōn hois aganois beleessin epoichomenos katepephne)
short: At Sunium Menelaus' helmsman Phrontis died suddenly at the steering-oar, killed by Apollo's 'gentle arrows': the Homeric way of describing a quick, painless death.
body: Merry and Riddell explain that sudden death without suffering was ascribed to the painless shafts of Apollo (for men) or Artemis (for women), contrasted with 'long disease' (11.172-173); Penelope prays for such a death from Artemis (18.202-204, 20.61-65). They add that it was not always a mercy, citing the anger of Artemis against Ariadne. Sunium, 'the cape of Athens' and 'holy' (hiron), is the southern tip of Attica; Merry and Riddell connect the epithet with the temple and with sailors' cult of Poseidon there. Menelaus delays to bury his comrade, a pious act that costs him his place beside Nestor; the storm off Malea then scatters his fleet to Crete and Egypt.

title: Crete: the Cydonians, Gortyn and Phaestus
greek: ἧχι Κύδωνες ἔναιον Ἰαρδάνου ἀμφὶ ῥέεθρα … ἐσχατιῇ Γόρτυνος … ἐς Φαιστόν (hēchi Kudōnes enaion Iardanou amphi rheethra …)
short: Part of Menelaus' fleet was wrecked on the south coast of Crete near Gortyn, by a headland toward Phaestus, where the south wind drives the waves.
body: Merry and Riddell explain the geography with Strabo's help. The Cydonians lived in western Crete, around the river Iardanus on the north coast, but their territory stretched across the island to the south, where the coast turns sharply to form a cape (the 'left headland'). Gortyn lay inland on the fertile plain south of Mount Ida, and Phaestus to its south-west. Both Gortyn and Phaestus have important Minoan and later remains. The Cydonians appear again in Odysseus' false description of Crete with its mixture of peoples (19.175-177). The precision of the description, down to 'a little rock holds back a great wave', suggests real local knowledge.

title: Orestes 'back from Athens' and the funeral feast
greek: ἂψ ἀπ᾽ Ἀθηνάων, κατὰ δ᾽ ἔκτανε πατροφονῆα … μητρός τε στυγερῆς καὶ ἀνάλκιδος Αἰγίσθοιο (aps ap' Athēnaōn, kata d' ektane patrophonēa … mētros te stugerēs kai analkidos Aigisthoio)
short: Orestes returns in the eighth year, kills Aegisthus, and holds a funeral feast for him and 'his hateful mother': the only hint in Homer of Clytemnestra's death.
body: Merry and Riddell note that that in the tragic legend Orestes came from Phocis, and that Aeschylus makes him go to Athens only after the killing; they refer the reader to the critical note on the reading 'from Athens'. The Odyssey avoids saying that Orestes killed his mother; it says only that he gave a funeral feast (taphos) over both, and the word 'hateful' (stugerē) leaves her fate implied. Some scholars think she took her own life in the Homeric version; others that the poet suppresses the matricide to keep Orestes an uncomplicated model for Telemachus. Menelaus arrives that very day with his treasure.

title: The tongues of the victims
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄγε τάμνετε μὲν γλώσσας, κεράασθε δὲ οἶνον (all' age tamnete men glōssas, keraasthe de oinon)
short: At nightfall Athena tells the Pylians to cut the victims' tongues and mix wine: the tongues are thrown into the fire with a libation to close the day's sacrifice.
body: Merry and Riddell ask whether tamnete means 'cut out' or 'cut up for sacrifice'. Comparing Attic comic usage ('the tongue is cut separately'), and a scholion that the tongue was given to the herald as a first-fruit, they argue that the tongues had already been set aside and are now cut and offered. Some interpreters thought the offering was to Hermes, god of speech, to whom a last libation was poured before sleep (7.137-138), but Merry and Riddell, following Nitzsch, think Poseidon, the god of the day, is meant. The guests rise and pour wine on the burning tongues (3.341).

title: Athena departs as a sea-eagle (phēnē)
greek: φήνῃ εἰδομένη· θάμβος δ᾽ ἕλε πάντας ἰδόντας (phēnēi eidomenē; thambos d' hele pantas idontas)
short: Athena leaves Pylos in the form of a phēnē, a large bird of prey, and the whole company is struck with amazement; Nestor recognizes her.
body: Merry and Riddell identify the phēnē from Aristotle's description (larger than an eagle, ash-coloured) as the sea-eagle or possibly the lammergeier. Unlike the compressed simile of 1.320, eidomenē here describes actual bodily likeness: Athena takes the bird's shape. This epiphany is public, unlike her quiet departure in Ithaca, and it confirms to Nestor that Telemachus has divine protection: 'if verily when thou art so young the gods follow thee to be thy guides' (3.375-376). Such bird-form departures of gods recur (Athena as a swallow at 22.240). The moment completes Athena's role as Mentor in Book 3; she will not accompany Telemachus to Sparta.

title: Tritogeneia
greek: Διὸς θυγάτηρ, κυδίστη Τριτογένεια (Dios thugatēr, kudistē Tritogeneia)
short: A title of Athena of uncertain meaning: 'born at Triton' (a stream or lake), 'born from the head', or 'third-born'; already obscure to the ancients.
body: Merry and Riddell report the ancient derivation from Triton, a stream in Boeotia flowing into Lake Copais, comparing Athena's title Alalkomenēis from Boeotian Alalcomenae, and note that Herodotus connects Lake Tritonis in Libya with Athena (4.179-180). A Cretan word trito, 'head', gave the explanation 'head-born', referring to her birth from Zeus' head, a story not mentioned in Homer. They link 'Triton' with water words such as Amphitrite. The title also appears in Hesiod (Theogony 895, 924). Nestor uses it in his recognition of the goddess and follows it with a prayer and a vow to sacrifice a heifer with gilded horns.

title: Nestor's seat on the polished stones
greek: ἐπὶ ξεστοῖσι λίθοισιν … λευκοί, ἀποστίλβοντες ἀλείφατος (epi xestoisi lithoisin … leukoi, apostilbontes aleiphatos)
short: At dawn Nestor sits on the white polished stones before his doors, where his father Neleus used to sit, holding a sceptre: the place of royal judgement and counsel.
body: The stones 'glistening as with oil' may have been smoothed by long use or actually anointed, as sacred stones sometimes were. Nestor sits where Neleus sat before him, a picture of continuity of rule that Ithaca lacks. The elders on the shield of Akhilleus sit on 'polished stones in a sacred circle' to give judgement (Iliad 18.503-504), and Alcinous' people meet in an agora with polished stone seats (8.6). The sceptre marks his authority. The scene is followed by a roll-call of his sons, Echephron, Stratius, Perseus, Aretus, Thrasymedes and Peisistratus, who prepare the sacrifice: an image of a well-ordered house in which sons serve their father.

title: Nestor's sacrifice and the women's 'sacred cry' (ololygē)
greek: αἱ δ᾽ ὀλόλυξαν θυγατέρες τε νυοί τε καὶ αἰδοίη παράκοιτις (hai d' ololuxan thugateres te nuoi te kai aidoiē parakoitis)
short: The fullest sacrifice scene in Homer: the gilded heifer, the washing, the barley, the hair cut and burned, the stunning blow, the women's ritual cry, and the shared meal.
body: Nestor vows a heifer 'broad of brow, unbroken' with gilded horns (3.382-384) and fulfils the vow next day. Each son has a role: Laerces the goldsmith gilds the horns; Stratius and Echephron lead the victim; Aretus brings water and barley; Thrasymedes stands with the axe; Perseus holds the bowl for the blood. Merry and Riddell stress that the ololygē is not a shriek of horror but a religious shout of joy at the consummation of the sacrifice, compared with Aeschylus (Agamemnon 595), and that the heifer is first stunned by the axe and only then has its throat cut by Peisistratus. Penelope raises the same cry in prayer (4.767), while Odysseus forbids Eurycleia to cry it over the dead suitors (22.411-412). Burkert's analysis of Greek sacrifice draws heavily on this passage.

title: Polycaste bathes Telemachus
greek: τόφρα δὲ Τηλέμαχον λοῦσεν καλὴ Πολυκάστη (tophra de Tēlemachon lousen kalē Polukastē)
short: Nestor's youngest daughter bathes and anoints the guest, an ordinary act of Homeric hospitality; a later tradition made her Telemachus' wife.
body: Bathing by women of the household is a routine courtesy to guests (as with Helen's maids in Sparta, 4.49-50, and Helen herself bathing the disguised Odysseus at Troy, 4.252). Merry and Riddell note that lousen has pluperfect force: she had bathed him meanwhile. Telemachus emerges 'in form like unto the immortals', a formula that marks his transformation. In the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women Polycaste bore Telemachus a son named Persepolis, a tradition that seems to grow out of this scene. The bath also prepares him for the next stage, his departure by chariot with Peisistratus.
